introductorius maior qui etiam arabice exstat, vertit Iohannes Hispalensis; qui liber
incipit revera verbis : Laus Deo, cf. Steinschneider, l. c., p. 360 a; Suter, op. cit.,
p. 29. — Legitur in praefatione libri Albumazar de magnis coniunctionibus (August,
Vindelic. 1489): Hic est liber ... editus a Japhar astrologo qui dictus est Albumasar.
1 ‘Abd-el’aziz ben ‘Otman el Qabiši vixit in urbe Mosul saeculo X exeunte,
Scripsit introductionem in artem astrologiae, quae in versione Iohannis Hispa-
lensis, saepius inde ab anno 1485 edita, incipit verbis Postulata a Domino; cf.
Steinschneider, l. c., p. 361, § 8; Suter, op. cit., p. 60, § 132.
2 Iudaeus Sahl ben Bischr vixit saeculo IX et scripsit Introductorium de princi-
piis iudiciorum quod simul cum Ptolemaei Quadripartito Venetiis a. 1493, 1519
editum est et verbis ss. incipit. De hoc scriptore et operibus eius, cf. Steinschnei-
der, Die hebraïschen Uebersetz. des Mittelalters, p. 603 ss.; Suter, op. cit., p. 15, § 26.
3 De Aristotelis libris qui ferebantur astrologicis, cf. Catal., I, p. 83, n. 3.
4 Sacratissimus astronomie Ptolemaei liber quem scripsit ad Heristhonem filium
suum, qui Venetiis a. 1509 typis mandatus est, incipit verbis : Signorum alia
utrum (sic) masculini generis alia feminini ; cf. Steinschneider, l. c., p. 383, § 40 c.
5 Tractatus Io. Hispalensis de signis caelestibus, incipiens verbis : In nomine
domini Creatoris. Cinctura firmamenti exstat in codice Vindobonensi, cf. Stein-
schneider, l. c., p. 373, § 33 d.
6 Liber novem iudicum est collectio astrologica ex arabicis auctoribus compilata
quae in nonnullis codicibus exstat et a. 1509 Venetiis, iterum a. 1571, edita est, cf.
Steinschneider, l. e., p. 394, § 50.

the greater introductory book which also exists in Arabic, John of Seville translated; which book
actually begins with the words: Laus Deo ('Praise to God'), cf. Steinschneider, l. c., p. 360 a; Suter, op. cit.,
p. 29. — It is read in the preface of the book of Albumazar on the great conjunctions (Augsburg,
1489): Hic est liber ... editus a Japhar astrologo qui dictus est Albumasar ('This is the book ... published by Japhar the astrologer who is called Albumasar').
1 ‘Abd-el’aziz ben ‘Otman el Qabiši lived in the city of Mosul at the end of the 10th century,
He wrote an introduction to the art of astrology, which in the version of John of Seville,
published quite often from the year 1485, begins with the words Postulata a Domino ('Requested from the Lord'); cf.
Steinschneider, l. c., p. 361, § 8; Suter, op. cit., p. 60, § 132.
2 The Jew Sahl ben Bischr lived in the 9th century and wrote the Introductorium de princi-
piis iudiciorum ('Introductory book on the principles of judgments') which was published together with Ptolemy's Quadripartitum at Venice in the years 1493, 1519
and begins with the following words. Concerning this writer and his works, cf. Steinschnei-
der, Die hebraïschen Uebersetz. des Mittelalters, p. 603 ss.; Suter, op. cit., p. 15, § 26.
3 Concerning the books of Aristotle which were circulated as astrological, cf. Catal., I, p. 83, n. 3.
4 The most sacred book of astronomy of Ptolemy which he wrote to Heristho his
son, which was committed to type at Venice in the year 1509, begins with the words: Signorum alia
utrum (sic) masculini generis alia feminini ('Of the signs some are of the masculine gender, others of the feminine'); cf. Steinschneider, l. c., p. 383, § 40 c.
5 The treatise of John of Seville on the celestial signs, beginning with the words: In nomine
domini Creatoris. Cinctura firmamenti ('In the name of the Lord the Creator. The girdle of the firmament') exists in the Viennese codex, cf. Stein-
schneider, l. c., p. 373, § 33 d.
6 The Liber novem iudicum ('Book of the nine judges') is an astrological collection compiled from Arabic authors
which exists in some codices and was published in the year 1509 at Venice, and again in the year 1571, cf.
Steinschneider, l. c., p. 394, § 50.

summary.headline: Astrological Introductory Works
summary.text: Catalogue of astrological introductory works by Abdilaziz (Alkabizi), Zahel, Aristotle, Ptolemy, John of Seville, and the Nine Judges, identified by their opening words and discussions of the twelve signs, masculine and feminine genders, and celestial circles. Notes discuss Arabic and Latin transmission, Albumasar, Sahl ben Bischr, Ptolemy’s Quadripartitum, and related printed editions and manuscripts.
